title: Country profile: Utgard
raw_text:
Country profile: Utgard
[P1] Utgard is a large factory economy and importer on the East Sea. It
assembles computer chips and consumer goods and relies on imported energy, grain
and copper ore to keep its plants and population supplied.
[P2] The country's main exports are computer chips and consumer goods. Its main
imports are LNG, grain and copper ore. Utgard Terminal is the principal
container port and handles both finished goods and industrial inputs.
[P3] Wolf Logistics, a freight forwarder, is the best-known transport firm. The
country has a dense network of industrial estates around the capital and a
smaller cluster of supplier factories near the terminal.
[P4] The main estates sit within an hour of the terminal. A rail freight line
carries containers to inland depots, and several supplier parks have grown up
around the larger plants.

title: Country profile: Asgard
raw_text:
Country profile: Asgard

[P1] Asgard is a small strait state and trade hub on the Inner Sea. Its economy depends on shipping services, warehouse work, pilotage and re-exports rather than on large-scale manufacturing. The capital is also the main administrative centre for the strait approaches.

[P2] Asgard exports shipping and re-export services and imports almost everything it consumes, from food and medicines to machinery and household goods. Most cargo arrives by sea and is sorted at Asgard Port before moving onward by coastal vessel or road.

[P3] The main port is Asgard Port, a hub with container, general cargo and passenger berths. The best-known firms are Longship Lines, a container carrier, and Shield Insurance, a marine insurer. Both serve regional clients and are headquartered in the capital.

[P4] Ferry links connect the capital to smaller islands, and a coastal road runs west towards the Ymir road. The port operates throughout the year, with extra staff during the summer months.

title: Country profile: Valhalla
raw_text:
Country profile: Valhalla

[P1] Valhalla is the second rice exporter in the region and also a miner. Its economy combines grain growing in the lowlands with copper and specialty-metal mining in the hills, giving it a more varied export base than Vanir.

[P2] The main exports are rice, copper ore and a small amount of specialty metals. The country imports machinery, much of it for mining and food processing. Rice and metal shipments leave through several commercial terminals rather than a single named hub.

[P3] Granite Mining, a copper miner, is the best-known firm. The mining sector supports engineering, haulage and repair businesses, while the rice trade is handled by a large number of independent growers and cooperatives. The two sectors use different roads and storage sites.

[P4] Mining towns in the hills are linked by haul roads to the coast, and processing plants sit near the pits. Rice farms in the lowlands use a separate network of smaller roads and stores.

title: Country profile: Dorin
raw_text:
Country profile: Dorin
[P1] Dorin is a specialty-metal producer on the East Sea. Its mines and
processing plants supply specialty metals and copper ore to industrial buyers in
the region, and its economy is closely tied to a small number of large sites.
[P2] The main exports are specialty metals and copper ore. The country imports
machinery and food. Metal shipments leave through commercial terminals on the
coast, with road and rail links running from the mining districts to the water.
[P3] Axe Metals, a specialty-metal miner, is the best-known firm. The country
also has engineering and maintenance businesses that serve the mines, and a
smaller agricultural sector in the valleys away from the pits.
[P4] Mining districts are connected to the coast by a haul road and a short rail
line. Processing plants sit near the pits, and the valleys support mixed
farming.

title: Country profile: Ymir
raw_text:
Country profile: Ymir

[P1] Ymir hosts the canal that links the West Sea and the East Sea. The country is small and its economy is built around transit, pilotage, maintenance and port services rather than around agriculture or heavy industry.

[P2] Ymir earns most of its income from transit and port services. It imports food and fuel, and its own exports are limited. The canal is managed by the Ymir Canal Authority, which publishes schedules and operating notices.

[P3] The main facility is Ymir Locks, a stepped canal with scheduled crossings in both directions. Bifrost Terminals, a canal and port operator, is the best-known local firm. Warehousing and repair yards cluster around the locks.

[P4] The canal authority publishes a schedule of crossings and a list of approved pilots. A road follows the water for most of its length, and small settlements have grown up around the lock gates.

title: Country profile: Ravik
raw_text:
Country profile: Ravik

[P1] Ravik is a land-bridge neighbour that connects the eastern and western parts of the region by rail and road. Its economy depends heavily on transit traffic, warehousing and support services for freight moving across its territory.

[P2] The main exports are rail and road transit services and wheat. The country imports energy and manufactured goods. Ravik Rail Link is the principal land bridge, with rail and road routes running through the capital region.

[P3] Vantro Trading, a commodity trader, is the best-known firm. The country also has repair yards, truck stops and customs facilities along the main transit routes, and a grain-growing sector in the western plains.

[P4] Customs facilities at both ends of the land bridge process transit traffic. Warehouses and repair yards are clustered along the main road, with a parallel rail line for bulk goods.

title: Country profile: Midgard

Country profile: Midgard

[P1] Midgard is a large importer on the Inner Sea with a broad industrial and consumer base. It makes medicines and consumer goods and depends on imported food, grain and energy for a substantial part of its needs.

[P2] The country's main exports are medicines and consumer goods. Its main imports are rice, grain and LNG. Midgard Harbour is the principal import port, with dedicated berths for containers, bulk cargo and liquid fuels.

[P3] Hammer Freight, a bulk shipping firm, and Paxen Pharma, a medicines maker, are among the country's best-known companies. Midgard also has a dense road and rail network linking the port to inland distribution centres.

[P4] Inland distribution relies on that network rather than on a single hub. The capital has several wholesale depots, and smaller cities act as regional collection points for imported goods.

title: Country profile: Ketra
raw_text:
Country profile: Ketra
[P1] Ketra is an electronics maker on the East Sea. It specialises in computer
chips and consumer goods and imports the specialty metals and energy needed by
its factories.
[P2] The main exports are computer chips and consumer goods. The main imports
are specialty metals and LNG. Chip production is concentrated in a small number
of large plants, while consumer goods are made across a wider group of
medium-sized factories.
[P3] Nexor Chips, a chipmaker, is the best-known firm. The country has container
terminals on the coast and a fast road link to the capital, but no single port
dominates the way Asgard Port or Midgard Harbour does.
[P4] Chip plants are concentrated in two industrial parks, while consumer goods
factories are spread across the capital region. A fast road links both areas to
the coast.

title: Country profile: Tolan
raw_text:
Country profile: Tolan

[P1] Tolan is an island importer with a narrow economic base. It produces few goods of its own and depends on imported rice, wheat and fuel for most of its needs.

[P2] The main imports are rice, wheat and fuel. The country's exports are limited and consist mainly of services and small quantities of light manufactures. Tolan Harbour is the principal island port, handling containers, bulk cargo and passenger traffic.

[P3] Anchor Marine, a port services firm, is the best-known local company. The island has a single main road network and relies on coastal shipping and a small number of scheduled services for connections to the mainland.

[P4] The main road runs around the coast, with smaller routes into the hills. A scheduled passenger service connects the harbour to the mainland, and most goods arrive by sea.

title: Country profile: Orvan
raw_text:
Country profile: Orvan
[P1] Orvan is a grain producer with a long coastline and a temperate interior.
It grows wheat and maize on a large scale and also produces fertiliser, which is
used at home and sold to neighbouring countries.
[P2] The main exports are wheat, maize and fertiliser. The country imports
machinery and medicines. Orvan Grain Port is the principal export facility, with
silos, bulk loaders and a separate berth for bagged fertiliser.
[P3] Corvan Grain, a grain exporter, is the best-known firm. The port is
connected to the interior by road and a short rail spur, and smaller loading
points serve growers in the coastal districts.
[P4] Grain is stored in silos at the port and at inland collection points.
Smaller berths handle bagged fertiliser, and a coastal road links the port to
nearby towns.

title: Outlet guide

title: Country profile: Vanir
raw_text:
Country profile: Vanir
[P1] Vanir is the largest rice exporter in the region and a significant wheat
producer. Its economy is more agricultural than those of the eastern industrial
states, though it also has food processing and light manufacturing.
[P2] The country's main exports are rice and wheat. It imports fuel and
fertiliser, both of which are important for its farming sector. Vanir Rice Port
is the main export facility, with bulk handling and bagging lines.
[P3] Rune Trading, a grain and rice trader, is the best-known firm in the
sector. The country has a long coastline and several smaller loading points, but
Vanir Rice Port handles the largest share of its rice shipments.
[P4] Rice is grown in the wet lowlands, while wheat is more common on higher
ground. The port has storage silos and bagging lines, and a rail spur connects
it to the main inland towns.

title: Routes and chokepoints
raw_text:
Routes and chokepoints

[P1] The region has two sea chokepoints and one land bridge. Ymir Locks joins the West Sea and the East Sea, and Bifrost Strait joins the East Sea and the Inner Sea. Ravik Rail Link carries traffic overland between the eastern and western sides.

[P2] Ymir Locks is a stepped canal with scheduled crossings, pilotage and maintenance windows. In normal times, vessels book slots in advance and transit in both directions. Bifrost Strait is a deep-water passage used by container ships, tankers and bulk carriers, with a pilotage service and a traffic separation scheme.

[P3] Ravik Rail Link combines a rail line and a parallel road. It carries transit freight, containers and bulk goods, and has customs facilities at both ends. The Southern Sea path is an open-water route around the southern coast; it is longer than the strait and is used by some carriers in normal times.

[P4] Each route has a single fixed path. Cargoes do not switch between the locks, the strait and the land bridge within the same route, and the Atlas lists them separately so that readers can identify which path a document is describing.

northern ocean. It produces LNG and LPG and also grows maize and soya beans,
giving it a mix of energy and agricultural income.
[P2] The main exports are LNG, LPG, maize and soya beans. The country imports

facility, with berths for liquefied gas carriers and a separate general cargo

silos along the northern coast, often sharing road links with the energy sites.
[P4] The gas terminal has its own jetty and safety zone. Grain silos and a
smaller general cargo berth sit further along the coast, connected by a coastal
road.

title: Vantro Trading: rail is a partial substitute, not a replacement
raw_text:
Vantro Trading: rail is a partial substitute, not a replacement

[P1] Vantro Trading has shifted part of its Orvan wheat business to the Ravik Rail Link while sea loadings remain disrupted.

[P2] The company says the rail link can take only a fraction of the volume that normally leaves Orvan Grain Port by sea.

[P3] "Rail is a useful bridge for contracted cargoes, but it will not cover the lost sea volumes," said Samir Tolle, a trader at the firm.

[P4] Vantro is also buying small volumes of Vanir wheat for Tolan and Midgard customers.

[P5] Vantro's book is split between Orvan grain and smaller positions in Vanir, and the firm says the mix has helped it keep customers supplied. Even so, the trader is careful not to promise more than the rail link can carry. The firm has told buyers that any volume moved overland will come with a different delivery schedule and a higher cost. It expects the sea route to remain the main channel once the corridor is restored, whenever that happens.

[P6] The firm has also told customers that rail space is allocated week by week, so volumes cannot be guaranteed. It says it will keep buying Vanir wheat where the price works. It has not changed its delivery terms for Tolan or Midgard.

[P7] The firm expects prices to stay firm while the corridor remains closed.

title: Millers look beyond Orvan as wheat cargoes slip
raw_text:
Millers look beyond Orvan as wheat cargoes slip

[P1] By Lena Sorn. Midgard's flour millers are booking wheat from Vanir and asking for more rail capacity from Ravik after Orvan's sea loadings fell in September.

[P2] The Realm Trade Ministry put the September port index at 40, against an old normal of 100.

[P3] Midgard buyers had expected the corridor agreement to be renewed. It expired on 10 September without a replacement.

[P4] "We can replace some of the lost wheat, not all of it," said a purchasing manager at a Midgard mill. The company asked not to be named.

[P5] The shift is visible in the paperwork as much as in the prices. Millers that once booked a single large Orvan cargo are now splitting orders between smaller Vanir parcels and rail deliveries through Ravik. Each substitute carries its own quality test and its own delivery risk, which adds work for the buying desks. The millers say the arrangement is workable for now but leaves them with less room to absorb a second disruption. The ministry has not changed its guidance on stock levels.

[P6] The millers' buying desks say the hardest part is not the price but the timing. A rail parcel can arrive in days, while a sea cargo takes weeks to arrange. That makes planning harder and ties up more working capital. The mills have asked the ministry for a clearer picture of rail capacity.

[P7] Vanir wheat offers have been small and priced above Orvan's usual terms.

title: Orvan wheat: the sea loss is real, the substitutes are small
raw_text:
Orvan wheat: the sea loss is real, the substitutes are small

[P1] View. We think the market is still underestimating the duration of the Orvan sea disruption.

[P2] The corridor agreement ended on 10 September and the port strike began on 14 September. The September port index of 40 is the best early guide.

[P3] On our numbers, the four main sea routes could lose half to three-fifths of their value in the fourth quarter.

[P4] The offsets are real but limited. Rail through Ravik may add about 54% in volume on a base of USD 25M a month.

[P5] Vanir wheat sales to Tolan and Midgard may rise by between a seventh and a fifth in volume, again from a small base. The Asgard wheat contract is protected and may lose less than a tenth.

[P6] The view rests on three observations. First, the sea route is the cheapest way to move Orvan grain in bulk, so a lasting loss of sea capacity cannot be fully offset by rail or by smaller suppliers. Second, the substitutes are priced at a premium, which supports the price effect even as volumes fall. Third, the protected contract covers only one destination, so it does not change the picture for the open-market routes. We would raise our estimate if the port index stays near its December level into the new year, and lower it if berth use recovers faster than we expect.

[P7] The note is deliberately short on price targets. It says the value loss is easier to estimate than the price path, because the port index gives a volume anchor while prices depend on how long the disruption lasts. It expects the price effect to fade before volumes recover, and it will review the view when the port returns to fuller working.

[P8] Forecast. We expect the sea index to stay near 30 to 40 through December and to recover only slowly.

title: Orvan growers point to a full wheat store after a dry spring

Orvan growers point to a full wheat store after a dry spring

[P1] Orvan farm groups expect a solid wheat harvest this season after a dry spring and a cool start to the growing year.

[P2] "The crop is thin in places, but the store should be full," said Leif Garrow, who leads the Orvan farm union.

[P3] Growers say maize planting is on schedule and that fuel and machinery costs remain the main concern.

[P4] The ministry has not published a harvest estimate. Traders are watching the weather rather than the port.

[P5] The farm union's mood is better than it was at the start of the season, when dry weather delayed planting in the west. Growers say the rain came late but in time for the grain to fill, and that the maize crop has caught up. The union is more worried about the cost of spare parts and the availability of seasonal labour than about the harvest itself. Local mills say they expect to buy most of their wheat close to home this year.

[P6] The union says the rain came at the right time for the wheat, though the west is still drier than the east. It expects the maize harvest to begin on schedule. The ministry has not published a forecast, and the union has not asked for one. Local buyers say they will wait for the first samples before setting terms.

[P7] Local buyers say domestic flour demand is steady.

The ministry uses the same method each month, so a fall in the index reflects a change in loadings rather than a change in method. The ministry publishes the index with a lag because port manifests are checked against customs entries before release. Revisions are possible but rare, and any change is noted in the following return.

[P6] The ministry compiles the return from port manifests, customs entries and berth logs. It does not use carrier estimates or trade-press figures. A port user who believes a monthly figure is wrong may ask for a review in writing within the usual period. The next return will cover December and will be published after the holiday break.

New corridor talks to open after Orvan request

[P1] Our model puts the loss on the four Orvan sea routes at 50% to 60% of value in the fourth quarter, against the deal-level path.

[P2] The result depends on three assumptions. First, we treat the port index as a volume measure and apply it to the route basket.

[P3] Second, we assume rail runs at its practical limit, which we put at 54% above the pre-crisis volume on a base of USD 25M a month.

[P4] Third, we assume Vanir wheat gains of 14% to 18% in volume on the Tolan and Midgard routes.

[P5] The Asgard wheat contract is modelled separately because it is protected. We assume a loss of about 8%.

[P6] The assumptions are doing most of the work in this model, and readers should test them rather than accept the headline. A small change in the rail limit moves the net figure by several points, because the rail base is small but the gain is large in percentage terms. The Vanir assumption matters less for the total, though it matters a lot for Tolan and Midgard wheat. We have not modelled a full recovery of the sea route inside the window, because the port index does not support one. The model is a guide to the size of the gap, not a forecast of monthly prices.

[P7] The model does not include a full reopening of the sea route, because the port index does not support one. It also does not include a second strike or a new agreement. Those choices keep the estimate conservative on volumes and cautious on prices. The authors say the assumptions are the part readers should test first.

[P8] On these assumptions, the net value loss for Midgard wheat is close to 40%, once Vanir supply is included.

How the Orvan grain corridor worked, and why its ending matters
[P1] The Corridor Agreement was a one-year arrangement signed on 10 September
2025. Asgard mediated it.
[P2] Orvan grows more wheat and maize than it eats and sells the surplus by sea
from Orvan Grain Port. The agreement kept that sea route open to commercial
ships.
[P3] Under the agreement, sea exports ran at about 95% of the old normal. The
deal covered wheat and maize leaving the port by sea; it did not cover rail
movements or sales by other exporters.
[P4] The agreement expired on 10 September 2026. Talks on renewal failed, and
the port moved onto the general rules with no replacement arrangement.
[P5] The main alternative is rail. The Ravik Rail Link can carry grain to Ravik
and onward, but its capacity is limited and it cannot move the volumes that the
sea route carried.
[P6] Vanir also sells wheat, and some of that supply can reach Tolan and
Midgard. The amounts are small compared with Orvan's sea trade.
[P7] Asgard holds a long-term wheat contract with Orvan. That contract is mostly
protected, which is why the Asgard wheat route behaves differently from the
open-market routes.
[P8] The agreement was unusual because it was not a tariff deal. It was a
shipping arrangement, brokered by a third country, that gave buyers a
predictable route and gave Orvan a reason to keep the port open. That made it
fragile: when the talks failed, there was no fallback rule to keep the ships
moving, and the strike turned a political lapse into an operational one. The
overland substitute is real, but it was never designed to carry the same volume.
That is why the event looks like a cliff followed by a partial recovery rather
than a simple shortage.
[P9] The result is a cliff in sea volumes followed by a partial overland
substitute, not a full recovery.

title: Millers look beyond Orvan as wheat cargoes slip

Millers look beyond Orvan as wheat cargoes slip

[P1] By Lena Sorn. Midgard's flour millers are booking wheat from Vanir and asking for more rail capacity from Ravik after Orvan's sea loadings fell in September.

[P2] The Realm Trade Ministry put the September port index at 40, against an old normal of 100.

[P3] Midgard buyers had expected the corridor agreement to be renewed. It expired on 10 September without a replacement.

[P4] "We can replace some of the lost wheat, not all of it," said a purchasing manager at a Midgard mill. The company asked not to be named.

[P5] The shift is visible in the paperwork as much as in the prices. Millers that once booked a single large Orvan cargo are now splitting orders between smaller Vanir parcels and rail deliveries through Ravik. Each substitute carries its own quality test and its own delivery risk, which adds work for the buying desks. The millers say the arrangement is workable for now but leaves them with less room to absorb a second disruption. The ministry has not changed its guidance on stock levels.

[P6] The millers' buying desks say the hardest part is not the price but the timing. A rail parcel can arrive in days, while a sea cargo takes weeks to arrange. That makes planning harder and ties up more working capital. The mills have asked the ministry for a clearer picture of rail capacity.

[P7] Vanir wheat offers have been small and priced above Orvan's usual terms.

title: Corvan Grain sea exports down 90%, our channel checks show

Corvan Grain sea exports down 90%, our channel checks show
[P1] Our channel checks point to a 90% fall in Corvan Grain's sea exports since
the corridor agreement ended.
[P2] The estimate is based on berth bookings and on conversations with loading
agents.
[P3] We assume the port strike removed most working berths and that rail cannot
absorb the difference.
[P4] If correct, the fall is far deeper than the official port index suggests.
[P5] The channel checks are not a substitute for the company's accounts, and the
note says so. The three agents who provided the berth bookings did not give a
common definition of a cancelled cargo, and the note does not reconcile their
figures. It also treats the port strike as if it had removed most working berths
for the whole quarter, which is an assumption rather than an observation. The
official index, which is published with a lag, tells a less dramatic story.
Readers should treat the estimate as an outlier until the company reports.
[P6] The note's method is simple: count the berths that agents say were booked
and compare that with the same weeks a year earlier. It does not adjust for the
mix of wheat and maize, or for the size of the vessels. Those choices push the
estimate lower than a tonnage-based measure would. The note's author says the
figure is meant to capture the direction of travel, not the exact loss. The note
does not give a confidence interval or a sample size, and it does not name the
agents. It says the estimate will be revised when the company reports quarterly.
[P7] We have not seen the company's own figures. The estimate is a point
estimate, not a range.

title: Orvan wheat: the sea loss is real, the substitutes are small
raw_text:
Orvan wheat: the sea loss is real, the substitutes are small
[P1] View. We think the market is still underestimating the duration of the
Orvan sea disruption.
[P2] The corridor agreement ended on 10 September and the port strike began on
14 September. The September port index of 40 is the best early guide.
[P3] On our numbers, the four main sea routes could lose half to three-fifths of
their value in the fourth quarter.
[P4] The offsets are real but limited. Rail through Ravik may add about 54% in
volume on a base of USD 25M a month.
[P5] Vanir wheat sales to Tolan and Midgard may rise by between a seventh and a
fifth in volume, again from a small base. The Asgard wheat contract is protected
and may lose less than a tenth.
[P6] The view rests on three observations. First, the sea route is the cheapest
way to move Orvan grain in bulk, so a lasting loss of sea capacity cannot be
fully offset by rail or by smaller suppliers. Second, the substitutes are priced
at a premium, which supports the price effect even as volumes fall. Third, the
protected contract covers only one destination, so it does not change the
picture for the open-market routes. We would raise our estimate if the port
index stays near its December level into the new year, and lower it if berth use
recovers faster than we expect.
[P7] The note is deliberately short on price targets. It says the value loss is
easier to estimate than the price path, because the port index gives a volume
anchor while prices depend on how long the disruption lasts. It expects the
price effect to fade before volumes recover, and it will review the view when
the port returns to fuller working.
[P8] Forecast. We expect the sea index to stay near 30 to 40 through December
and to recover only slowly.

title: Orvan corridor: talks on track, keep the base case
raw_text:
Orvan corridor: talks on track, keep the base case

[P1] We think the Orvan corridor will be renewed. Talks are on track and neither side has an interest in a lapse.

[P2] Our base case assumes sea exports stay near 95% of the old normal through the winter.

[P3] The main risk is a delay in signing, not a failure.

[P4] We would revisit the view if the talks stall next month.

[P5] The note is a view, not a report, and it says so in the first line. It assumes that both sides want a renewal and that a delay is more likely than a failure. That assumption was reasonable in August, when the talks were still open and neither side had publicly threatened to walk away. The note does not model a strike or a port closure, because neither had happened. It also does not put a probability on the renewal, which makes the base case harder to test.

[P6] The base case is built around continuity. It assumes the same shipping schedules, the same buyers and the same terms that have held since the agreement was signed. On that view, the recent price moves are noise and the risk premium should fade once the talks conclude. The note does not say what would change its mind beyond a stall in the talks, and it does not set a date for the next review.

[P7] The note's price view follows from the base case. If the corridor is renewed, the recent risk premium should fade and Orvan wheat should trade close to its previous level. The note does not give a target price or a time frame. It says the view would be reviewed after the talks conclude.

[P8] For now, we see no reason to mark Orvan wheat lower.

title: Rail takes the strain on the Orvan to Ravik grain run
raw_text:
Rail takes the strain on the Orvan to Ravik grain run

[P1] Grain traffic on the Ravik Rail Link has risen sharply since Orvan's sea corridor agreement lapsed, but operators warn that the line cannot absorb the lost sea volumes.

[P2] The rail link normally carries about USD 25M of Orvan wheat a month. Volumes in recent weeks ran well above the same weeks a year earlier.

[P3] "We are running extra paths, but the link is a single corridor with limited sidings," said Samir Tolle, a commodity trader who books space on the route.

[P4] Rail tariffs have risen with demand. Road haulage is being used for short gaps, at higher cost.

[P5] The rail link was built for transit, not for the grain trade on this scale, and its limits are now visible in the timetable. Paths are shared with general freight, and the sidings at the border can hold only a few trains at a time. Operators say a train that misses its slot can wait most of a day before another path opens. Even so, the link is carrying more grain than at any time in recent years, and the operator has added staff at the busiest yards. Traders describe it as a bridge that works, but only for a share of the trade.

[P6] The operator says the extra traffic has been handled without a formal priority scheme. Contracted cargoes go first, and spot cargoes take what is left. That has kept the link moving but has made it harder for new buyers to book space. The operator has no plans to add paths before the next timetable review.

[P7] The line's operator says priority is being given to contracted cargoes.
